---
title: "Past data and few-unit designs"
description: "Analysing a design whose dates have passed, designing for a handful of markets, and the synthetic-control design that is planned but not built"
---

## Analyse past data

Sometimes the question is about something that already happened: *did last
spring's flash sale work?* The data exists, but nobody registered a plan
before it ran. Oxygen can still analyse it, under a label that makes its
standing clear.

### When it is offered

Write the design as you would for a new experiment, with the dates on which
the change actually happened, and price it. Its registration deadline has
passed, so the page shows **Registration refused** with the reason. Once all
of the design's dates are in the past, the same page offers **Analyse past
data** (workspace owners and admins), with this explanation:

> All of this design's dates are in the past. The result will be labelled
> "not pre-registered": it is exploratory, not a registered test, and no
> levers are switched.

It is refused while any day of the last after window is still to come.

### A rollout that was not randomised

When the change was rolled out to units someone chose (a feature switched on for
some listings, a policy applied to some stores), say so: under **Lever**, choose
**Already changed**. The form then asks for no automations. Under **Assignment**,
add one wave for each date the change went live, with the units it reached; every
other unit becomes the comparison. No seed is needed and pricing is optional. When
pricing cannot size the design (too little history), the report says **MDE
unavailable** with pricing's reason instead of refusing to read the data.

The report's **Randomisation** check then reads **Observational**: the treated and
comparison units were not drawn at random, so they may differ in ways other than
the change. If you edit a priced design's waves by hand, the same check reads
**Written by hand**.

### Units with missing data

When reading past data, a unit with too little data (fewer than the design's coverage
floor of the days, 90% by default) is left out, and a listed unit with no data at all is
left out of its group. Neither stops the analysis or removes days for the other units.
The report lists each one under **Dropped units, waves or pairs**, with the reason.

### A share as the outcome

To measure a share per unit (for example merchant-fulfilled units out of all units
sold), set **Divided by** under **Outcome**. Each unit's share is its total of the
outcome measure over its total of this one in each window, so a busy day counts for
more than a quiet one. Shares are analysed from past data only for now, and the report
gives no total for them.

### When the analysis is refused

If the analysis is refused (for example, a unit listed in a wave has no data), fix
the design or the data and choose **Analyse past data** again. A refused analysis
leaves no result, so the design stays editable; an analysis that produced a result
is final.

### What is different from a registered run

| | Registered run | Analyse past data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Levers | Switched on and off on schedule | **Never touched**; no automation runs |
| Confirming switches | Checked in the data | Not measured, since Oxygen made no switches |
| Guardrails | Watched hourly | None |
| Control group | Fixed shortly after registration | Fixed from the design's own before window: units with data then, never units that appeared later |
| Report label | **Registered result** | **RETROSPECTIVE — not pre-registered** |
| Slope proposed to the semantic model | When the guards pass | **Never** |

The run is created directly in the closing state, the design is locked like
any other, and the estimate runs as soon as possible. An experiment has one
run, so a design analysed from past data cannot also be registered; duplicate
it to run it for real.

### Why it is labelled the way it is

Writing the plan before the data exists is what entitles a registered
experiment to a plain significance test. A design written after the fact had
no such protection. Its author may, without meaning to, have chosen the
windows, the units or the measure that made the past look best. So the
report always leads with *"RETROSPECTIVE — not pre-registered: the design
was written after its data existed, so this is an exploratory reading, not a
registered test"*. And a slope found after the fact is a candidate to test,
not a coefficient to write into the model.

<Tip>
Use past-data runs to decide **what to test next**. If a retrospective read
looks promising, duplicate the experiment, move the dates forward and run
it registered.
</Tip>

## Designing for a few units

Geographic tests often have only a couple of dozen markets, and a chain may
have only a handful of stores it controls. With few units, the luck of the
draw matters a lot: one random split can put the three biggest markets on
the same side, and those three then decide the result. Four tools help.

### Matched pairs

**Match in pairs** sorts the units by their recent average, pairs neighbours
in that ranking, and flips a coin within each pair. Every pair puts one unit
on each side, so a lopsided draw is impossible. With 24 markets you get 12
pairs, 12 treated and 12 controls; an odd unit out becomes a control. It
needs at least four units.

### Staggered waves with a few held back

When some units must get the change and others cannot (for example,
company-owned stores against franchises), staggering the owned stores over
two or three waves, with any others held back, keeps a control on every date.
It usually prices close to a single wave of the same size.

### Groups

If single units are too noisy, randomise whole groups. This only helps when
there are still enough groups: the sample becomes the number of groups.

### Switchback

If no unit can be held back at all, the whole fleet can alternate. It needs
at least six pairs of periods at a significance level of 0.05, or four at a
directional 0.2.

<Note>
Pricing puts these side by side on your data. With few units the honest
answer is sometimes that nothing can detect the effect you expect. Pricing
will say so, which is far cheaper than finding out after the run.
</Note>

## Synthetic control (designed, not built)

<Warning>
This design is a **proposal under review**. It is not available in the
product. It is described here so stakeholders can see where few-unit and
non-random designs are heading.
</Warning>

Every design available today needs a random element: units held back at
random, or periods alternated at random. Two real cases have neither:

1. **A campaign that runs in places someone chose.** The brand team picks
   Denver for a launch. Nothing was randomised, so there is no control group,
   and the business will not alternate a live campaign week by week.
2. **A past campaign that was never registered** and was not randomised
   either.

**Synthetic control** builds the missing comparison from the units that were
not touched. For the treated market, it finds a weighted blend of untouched
markets (say 40% Phoenix, 35% Dallas, 25% Kansas City) whose sales tracked
the treated market's sales closely over a long period before the campaign.
After the campaign starts, that blend shows what the treated market would
probably have done without it. The effect is the gap between the two.

How it is planned to work:

- **The fit is the evidence.** The blend is fitted on a long before window,
  and the report shows the weights and how closely the blend tracked the
  treated unit before the change. If no blend tracks it well, the design is
  refused: the "effect" would just be the fit's error.
- **Is the gap unusual?** The same fit is repeated pretending each untouched
  market was the treated one. If the real market's gap stands out among those
  placebo gaps, the effect is real.
- **Pricing works as usual.** Effects of known size are planted at past dates
  to find the smallest effect the design can detect.
- **Clearly labelled.** A synthetic-control result would be labelled as *not
  randomised*, and pricing would rank a randomised design above it whenever
  both are possible. It also cannot hold when the change spills into the
  donor markets, such as a national TV burst, and the report would say so.

The first version is planned for geographic donors only; using other
products as donors for a single-product campaign is a follow-up.
